analysis.one_liner: Requires documentary proof of citizenship to register and photo ID to vote in federal elections.
analysis.headline: Introduced Jan. 29, 2026 with 49 of 53 Senate Republicans cosponsoring; referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, where no vote has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the National Voter Registration Act so that no one can register to vote in a federal election without showing documentary proof of U.S. citizenship — a passport, a REAL ID that marks citizenship, a military ID with a service record, a government photo ID showing U.S. birth, or a photo ID paired with a certified birth certificate or naturalization papers. It would also require a tangible photo ID to vote, including a copy submitted twice by absentee voters, and require states to run ongoing citizenship-verification programs using Homeland Security and Social Security data and to remove noncitizens from the rolls. Election officials who register someone without proof would face criminal penalties, private parties could sue over violations, and all of it would take effect immediately on enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: No group of voters gains anything material — the bill adds requirements rather than benefits. Supporters say the gain is confidence that only citizens are registered and voting. The interests positioned to gain are incumbent officeholders and party organizations, since every added document step raises the cost of registering and voting for the electorate at large.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits states from accepting or processing an application to register to vote in a federal election unless the applicant presents documentary proof of U.S. citizenship.
Requires a tangible photo ID to vote in person in a federal election, and requires absentee voters to submit a copy of their photo ID with both the ballot request and the ballot itself.

Requires each state to run an ongoing program identifying noncitizens on the voter rolls using information from the Department of Homeland Security's SAVE system, the Social Security Number Verification Service, or state license agencies, and to remove noncitizens from the rolls.
Creates a private right of action for violations and criminal penalties, including for election officials who register an applicant who does not present citizenship proof.

Includes accommodations for some groups: tribal IDs and the DHS 'KIC' American Indian Card count as proof, states must set up an alternative attestation process for applicants who cannot produce documents, and a construction rule preserves the right to cast a provisional ballot pending citizenship verification.

analysis.who_pays: Citizens who do not have a passport or an ID that marks citizenship would have to obtain qualifying documents — often a certified birth certificate meeting the bill's detailed requirements (issued in the state of birth, listing a parent's full name, bearing a seal and filing date), a naturalization certificate, or other listed papers — with mail and online registrants required to present them in person at an election office. States and counties would bear the cost of building verification and purge programs, and election officials would take on legal exposure, including criminal penalties and private lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters without citizenship-marking documents, and election offices

drawbacks.text: A REAL ID counts as proof only if it indicates the holder is a citizen, so many citizens would need a passport, a birth certificate meeting detailed content requirements (issued in the state of birth, listing a parent's full name, bearing a seal and filing date), a naturalization certificate, or another listed document — and the bill takes effect immediately on enactment, with no phase-in.

Applicants using the federal mail registration form — the remote registration method created by the 1993 law — would no longer be registered by mailing the form; they must present their citizenship documents in person to an election official by the registration deadline, or at the polling place in same-day-registration states.
Absentee voters would have to mail a copy of their photo ID twice: once with the ballot request and again with the ballot.

States must stand up citizenship-verification programs within 30 days of enactment, drawing on DHS and Social Security data with federal agencies required to answer within 24 hours, and DHS must investigate whether to open removal proceedings against any noncitizen found registered.

Election officials face criminal penalties for registering an applicant without citizenship proof, and private parties can sue — meaning offices may respond by rejecting registrations that raise any documentation question.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — keeping noncitizens off the voter rolls — is already covered by existing law: the federal registration form requires a citizenship attestation under penalty of perjury, and voting by a noncitizen is a federal crime. This bill's mechanism is different: it applies documentary proof demands to every registrant and photo ID demands to every voter, so the burden falls on eligible citizens by design, heaviest on those without a passport, with documents that don't reflect a current name, or who register by mail or vote absentee. The alternative attestation process exists, but it leaves the final judgment to officials who face penalties and lawsuits for getting it wrong. Whether that trade is worth it is the honest question, and the immediate effective date gives states no time to prepare.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which has taken no further action on it; no vote has been held while this Congress continues.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the bill on Jan. 29, 2026, joined on introduction by Sens. Scott of Florida, Budd, Banks, and Moody.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
49 of the Senate's 53 Republicans signed on as cosponsors.
No Democratic senator cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no further steps — no committee markup, no floor vote — since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has been enacted, so eligible voters who would face the new document requirements still register and vote under current rules. The bill's 49 Republican cosponsors hold the option of forcing a floor vote, but so far no one has won and no one has lost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Voters who lack citizenship-marking IDs, so far

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited four original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on Jan. 29, 2026 and has taken no further action on it — no markup, no vote.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill; the party's senators opposed the House-passed SAVE Act in the prior Congress.

sides.party_line_note: 49 of 53 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill; not one of the 45 Senate Democrats did.

industries.note: The bill hands election offices new duties — in-person document checks, citizenship-verification programs, roll purges — plus legal exposure, including criminal penalties for registering someone without proof and a private right of action. Those pressures push offices toward rejecting questionable registrations, which cuts against voter access even as the offices exist to serve voters.

The bill adds document, in-person, and mailing requirements to registration and voting with an immediate effective date. Every added step raises the cost of participating for the electorate at large, which tends to work in favor of the people already holding office.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Rules and Administration Committee with no markup or vote scheduled. Moving it would require a floor vote that needs 60 senators to cut off debate; with 49 Republican cosponsors and none from the other party, it would need at least a dozen Democratic votes it does not currently have. Similar proof-of-citizenship legislation passed the House in 2025 but stalled in the Senate, so the likely path is continued inaction unless leadership decides to force a vote it may not win.
